title: GitHub Security Best Practices: Protecting Your Code and Credentials
excerpt: Leaked credentials in Git commits have caused some of the largest data breaches in history. This guide covers how to secure your GitHub account and prevent secrets from ever hitting your repositories.
content:
The Stakes: What's at Risk

GitHub security isn't just about your personal account. Leaked API keys, database credentials, and AWS access keys committed to repositories have led to multi-million dollar cloud bills, data breaches affecting millions of users, and significant legal liability. In 2022, a developer accidentally committed Heroku OAuth tokens to a public repository — the resulting breach affected thousands of applications.

The good news: most GitHub security failures are preventable with the right configuration and habits. This guide covers both account security and the more critical issue of keeping secrets out of your code.

Account Security Basics

Start with a strong, unique password for your GitHub account — use our password generator to create a 20+ character random password and store it in a password manager. Never reuse your GitHub password anywhere else; GitHub credentials are extremely valuable to attackers.

Enable two-factor authentication immediately. GitHub now requires 2FA for all accounts that contribute to code. Go to Settings → Password and authentication → Enable two-factor authentication. Use an authenticator app (not SMS), and save your recovery codes somewhere secure. GitHub also supports hardware security keys (YubiKey) for the strongest possible protection.

Review authorized OAuth apps and personal access tokens. Go to Settings → Applications (OAuth Apps) and Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens. Remove any apps you no longer use and revoke any tokens you don't recognize or that have broader permissions than needed.

Never Commit Secrets to a Repository

This is the most critical GitHub security issue. A 'secret' includes: API keys, passwords, database connection strings, private keys, OAuth tokens, and environment variables containing sensitive values.

Once a secret is committed to a Git repository — even if you immediately delete it in the next commit — it remains in the Git history. If the repository was ever public (even briefly), bots scan GitHub continuously and will have captured it within seconds. Always treat a leaked secret as permanently compromised and rotate it immediately.

Use environment variables. Store secrets in environment variables, not in source code. In your application, read them with process.env.API_KEY (Node.js), os.environ['API_KEY'] (Python), or the equivalent for your language. On servers, set these in your hosting platform's environment configuration, never in the codebase.

Use .env files with .gitignore. Create a .env file locally for development secrets. Immediately add '.env' to your .gitignore before creating the file. Create a .env.example file that shows the structure with placeholder values — this is safe to commit.

Detecting and Fixing Leaked Secrets

If you suspect you've committed a secret, here's what to do:

  1. Rotate the credential immediately. Go to the service (AWS console, Stripe dashboard, etc.) and revoke or regenerate the exposed key. Do this before anything else — assume it's already been captured.
  2. Remove it from the code by replacing it with an environment variable reference.
  3. Clean the Git history using git-filter-repo (preferred over the deprecated BFG Repo-Cleaner). Run: git filter-repo --path-glob '*.env' --invert-paths or use git filter-repo --replace-text replacements.txt to scrub specific values.
  4. Force-push and notify collaborators that they need to re-clone — their local copies still have the secret in history.

Prevention tools: Install git-secrets (aws-labs/git-secrets) or gitleaks to scan commits before they're made. Many CI/CD pipelines can also run gitleaks to catch leaks before merging.

SSH Keys vs. HTTPS Authentication

For cloning and pushing to repositories, use SSH keys rather than HTTPS with a password. SSH keys are more secure and more convenient. To set up:

  1. Generate a key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com" (Ed25519 is the current recommended algorithm)
  2. Add a passphrase when prompted — this protects the key if your machine is compromised
  3. Add the public key to GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste the contents of your .pub file
  4. Test: ssh -T git@github.com

Store the SSH key passphrase in your password manager. Use ssh-agent so you don't have to type it constantly: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.

Repository and Organization Settings

  • Enable GitHub secret scanning. For public repos it's automatic. For private repos, go to Settings → Security → Secret scanning and enable it. GitHub will alert you when known secret patterns are detected.
  • Enable push protection. Settings → Security → Push protection. This blocks pushes that contain detected secrets before they're committed.
  • Set appropriate repository visibility. Default new repositories to private. Only make repositories public deliberately.
  • Review collaborator access regularly. Remove anyone who no longer needs access. Use the principle of least privilege — contributors should only have the access level they actually need.

Recommended Tools

For storing the passwords and tokens associated with your developer accounts, 1Password has excellent CLI integration that lets you inject secrets from your vault directly into shell sessions without ever writing them to disk. NordPass is a strong option for individuals managing multiple developer accounts. Visit our recommended tools page for full comparisons.
